Holomorphic boundaries and analytic directions

Written by GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI), October 2026. Public domain (CC0).

A holomorphic function can diverge as it approaches a real boundary and still have a distributional boundary value. The allowed imaginary directions then constrain the singular Fourier directions of that distribution. We prove the constraint at analytic regularity, retaining both the polynomial boundary growth and the uniform bounds required of the compact witness sequence. A family of linear poles will show that the resulting orientation is exact. Local wedges with polynomial bounds on each smaller cone have one common boundary and the same directional constraint.

The prerequisites are Holomorphic boundaries in convex cones, Theorem 2.1, Corollary 2.2 and its polydisk Cauchy proof; Derivative growth and finite-order localization, Theorem 4 and Lemma 5; and Cones and derivative-growth wavefronts, the analytic wavefront definition and projection theorem. We also use the complete one-variable pole formulas in Cauchy kernels and distributional boundary limits, Section 4. Their supplied scalar and integration foundations justify the ordinary product rule, compact integrals, affine changes of variables and limiting arguments below.

Exercises with complete solutions

Exercise 1 — elementary cone geometry (foundation). Compute the duals of the positive quadrant in , the half-space cone , and . State the respective restrictions given by (10).

Solution. For the quadrant, a vector with both coordinates nonnegative has nonnegative pairing with every positive vector. If one coordinate is negative, make that positive coordinate of large and hold the other fixed to obtain a negative pairing. Thus the dual is the closed positive quadrant. For , unrestricted tangential coordinates force every dual vector's tangential components to be zero: choose a sufficiently large tangential coordinate with opposite sign otherwise. The remaining condition is . Its dual is therefore . Finally, nonnegativity against both and for all forces every component to vanish, so the full-space dual is . Remove zero from each dual in (10): the restrictions are respectively the nonzero closed quadrant, the positive normal ray, and the empty set. Each conclusion requires the actual radial growth hypothesis on its stated cone.

Exercise 2 — a common boundary on opposite cones (intermediate). Suppose and satisfy the theorem on the cones and , over the same real base, and have the same boundary distribution . Prove that is real analytic throughout that base.

Solution. Theorem 2 places in the intersection of the two nonzero dual cones. A vector in has zero pairing with every . Since is open, choose and small with for each coordinate vector. Subtracting their zero pairings gives for every ; thus . The nonzero intersection is empty. The analytic wavefront projection theorem now gives empty analytic singular support, so is real analytic. This proves a statement about the common boundary; no larger holomorphic continuation domain has been presumed.

Exercise 3 — a bounded cutoff is not enough (advanced). Construct smooth cutoffs with one compact support, equal to one near zero and satisfying for , for which is not bounded as compact distributions. Explain the role of the second line of (6).

Solution. Use the controlled-cutoff theorem twice on disjoint intervals to obtain near zero and near two, with compact supports respectively close to zero and two. Choose the intervals so near two and near zero. Put . Its support is fixed, it equals one near zero, and its zeroth-order norm is uniformly bounded. Leibniz' rule gives, for , a sum bounded by ; the same form bounds the added term. However and . The definition of the distributional derivative yields . A single fixed test with has unbounded pairing, so this sequence is not even weakly bounded. The second line of (6) prevents this fixed-order derivative growth and is exactly what allows the finite-order bound for to control all products uniformly.

Exercise 4 — reflecting the pole (intermediate). Compute the analytic wavefront sets of and . Explain why adding the upper and lower poles has different directional behavior from either summand alone.

Solution. Complex conjugation of the upper pole gives the lower pole, because it conjugates the functions at positive height and their distributional limits. Conjugation reflects wavefront covectors by Exercise 2 of the preceding wavefront lesson. Formula (17) therefore gives only the negative ray over zero for . The pole formulas give . Away from zero, this principal value is the analytic function . At zero it has no continuous representative, by the unbounded restriction away from zero used above. It is real, so the preceding conjugation argument makes its analytic wavefront set symmetric. Projection provides at least one direction; symmetry and conicity provide both. Thus . The sum gathers the two possible orientations, consistently with the wavefront inclusion for sums.

Exercise 6 — two wedges with a common ray (intermediate). Suppose two local wedges over , with cones and , satisfy Theorem 3 and have the same boundary . Determine the resulting analytic-wavefront bound. Give an example attaining its allowed directions.

Solution. Their duals are respectively and . To verify either equality, nonnegative coordinate products give sufficiency; a coordinate with the wrong sign is exposed by increasing the corresponding allowed coordinate of while holding the other fixed. Apply (B4) twice and intersect. The result is The same holomorphic function works in both wedges, with the strict-cone bounds just proved. Exercise 7 — a smooth term with two analytic directions (advanced). On , set for and for . Prove that it is smooth, that it is not analytic at zero, and that its analytic wavefront over zero consists of both nonzero directions. Use the zero holomorphic function on the upper half-plane to explain the last sentence of Corollary 4.

Solution. On the positive half-line every derivative is a polynomial in times , by induction with the product and chain rules. For every , : writing , use with an integer . The same bound with one extra inverse power makes each difference quotient at zero tend to zero. Induction therefore extends all derivatives continuously across zero, with . The function is smooth.

If it were analytic at zero, its convergent Taylor series there would be zero and would make it vanish on a neighborhood, contradicting for . The analytic-wavefront projection theorem consequently gives at least one analytic singular direction over zero. Since is real, the conjugation identity reflects that direction; positive conicity then supplies both rays. Its smooth wavefront is empty. For on the upper half-plane the boundary is zero and the allowed nonzero dual cone is the positive ray. Adding produces a negative analytic direction as well, although (B6) remains valid with both smooth wavefronts empty.
